newsitem.title: UK: Euro Products Outlook - Mogas firm, others buckle.
newsitem.headline: Euro Products Outlook - Mogas firm, others buckle.

text.p: European oil product markets are set for a mixed week with gasoline seasonally firm but most of the barrel weak, traders said.
Gasoline should build on gains made late last week.
"I feel its pretty strong close up with room for more strength," said one dealer who said a number of the key players had long swaps positions and were bullish for the June period.
Prompt gasoline may be able to gain $1-2 a tonne to touch $210 for unleaded fob NWE cargoes although further out levels remain under pressure with July swaps backwardated up to $6 a tonne.
The arbitrage to the U.S looked increasingly attractive with at least one U.K cargo likely to head transatlantic.
Despite gasoline's potential strength, other oil products were mostly beginning to falter. Low sulphur diesel was seen under pressure from ample Mediterranean supply.
"EN590 is under pressure," said one trader. "We're seeing Med cargoes going north and there's even potential for U.S. material to make its way here."
An Algerian cargo was seen offered into the region at a premium of June IPE +$7.0 cif NWE on Friday, while EN590 barges traded at June IPE +$9.50 and +$9.25 fob ARA.
Heating oil was seen supported by demand out of Switzerland. German demand should pick up following the lull in trade due to last Thursday's regional Corpus Christi holiday.
Some players noted, however, that a lack of suitable storage in the region might pressure 0.2 percent premiums if traders were forced to sell material off on a prompt basis.
Naphtha was expected to ease slightly as an increase in June demand failed to materialise. On Friday buyers and sellers were apart with prices for cargoes at around $180/$185 cif NWE.
"I think there's more availability than demand at the moment," said one trader.
Fuel oil appeared to be on the brink of a tumble again, though traders noted high sulphur quality has defied downward pressure successfully since hitting its bottom in March.

"When crude weakened earlier last week we saw numbers in the $70 range appearing and that may happen again," said one trader. Local demand in the ARA was still just good enough to provide support at around the $80 level.
However, one percent swaps weakened on Friday, clearing the way for a fall in physical prices this week. The last cargo deal was two weeks ago and fresh material has been quietly becoming prompter.
"Every one was keeping very quiet about their material," said another trader, who noted that buying interest was muted.
Waves of Russian material have crashed down on north European and Mediterranean markets recently but the flow has eased for the moment.
Cracked fuel has predominated and scarce good quality straight-run is still attracting solid premia.
